```{python}
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]
probe_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] == "mechanism_probe"]

shape_labels = {
    "model_baseline_32x32": "M  32×32 baseline",
    "ai_wide_16x64": "M  16×64",
    "ai_extreme_8x128": "M  8×128",
    "ai_compact_32x16": "M  32×16",
    "conventional_baseline_32x32": "H  32×32 baseline",
    "heuristic_16x64": "H  16×64",
    "heuristic_8x128": "H  8×128",
    "heuristic_64x16": "H  64×16",
}

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.6, 2.65), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.22, right=0.985, top=0.82, bottom=0.22, wspace=0.42)

labels = [shape_labels[r["candidate_id"]] for r in arm_runs]
scores = [r["decision_score"] / 1000 for r in arm_runs]
colors = [COLORS["blue"] if r["arm"] == "model" else COLORS["green"] for r in arm_runs]
y = list(range(len(arm_runs)))
ax1.barh(y, scores, color=colors, height=0.66)
ax1.set_yticks(y, labels)
ax1.invert_yaxis()
ax1.set_xlabel("local score (thousands; lower is better)\nM = model proposals; H = fixed heuristic", fontsize=6.5)
ax1.set_title("Equal simulator-event allocation", fontsize=7, pad=5)
for yi, score in zip(y, scores):
    ax1.text(score + 0.8, yi, f"{score:.1f}", va="center", fontsize=5.5, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax1.set_xlim(0, max(scores) * 1.18)

probe = {}
for run in probe_runs:
    workload = "transposed" if "transposed" in run["candidate_id"] else "original"
    shape = f'{run["array_rows"]}×{run["array_cols"]}'
    probe[(shape, workload)] = run["decision_score"] / 1000

x = [0, 1]
for shape, color, marker in [("16×64", COLORS["blue"], "o"), ("64×16", COLORS["orange"], "s")]:
    values = [probe[(shape, "original")], probe[(shape, "transposed")]]
    ax2.plot(x, values, marker=marker, markersize=4.2, linewidth=1.5, color=color, label=shape)
    for xi, value in zip(x, values):
        # Labels sit beside the markers, outboard of the lines, to clear the
        # spine, the markers, and the other series.
        dx = -0.09 if xi == 0 else 0.09
        dy = -1.6 if (shape == "16×64" and xi == 1) else 1.4
        ax2.text(xi + dx, value + dy, f"{value:.1f}", ha="right" if xi == 0 else "left",
                 va="center", fontsize=5.5, color=color)

ax2.set_xticks(x, ["original", "M/N swapped"])
ax2.set_xlim(-0.45, 1.45)
ax1.text(-0.30, 1.08, "(a)", transform=ax1.transAxes, fontsize=7, fontweight="bold",
         color=COLORS["ink"])
ax2.text(-0.30, 1.08, "(b)", transform=ax2.transAxes, fontsize=7, fontweight="bold",
         color=COLORS["ink"])
ax2.set_ylabel("local score (thousands)", fontsize=6.5)
ax2.set_title("Mechanism probe: no reversal", fontsize=7, pad=5)
ax2.set_ylim(18, 61)
ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, loc="upper right")

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
    ax.grid(axis="x" if ax is ax1 else "y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)
    for spine in ["top", "right"]:
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

The $16 \times 64$ candidate tied the $32 \times 32$ baseline exactly on the recorded compute-window score (13,917 cycles excluding prefetch at 41.2% mean layer utilization, a score of 33.8k), and the fixed heuristic arm reached the same best score within the same four runs. No candidate improved on the baseline by the preregistered 1% margin, so the architecture outcome is null, the comparison shows no model advantage, and the retained recommendation is to keep the $32 \times 32$ baseline and stop this bounded search. A tie on the evaluation score validates neither an improvement nor the model's directional explanation. The proposal ranking and the mechanism probe answer different questions; an architectural loop must isolate causal claims with targeted diagnostic checks rather than relying on generative rationale.

Generation, tree search, and agent coordination provide ways to construct and revise candidates. The checks determine which artifacts satisfy the required properties and whether proposed mechanisms hold up under empirical testing. Even if construction reliably produces valid candidates, the study may have too many alternatives to evaluate. It then needs a search policy that directs where to allocate the remaining tool budget.

## Search Tactics and Budget Allocation {#sec-search-tactics-budget-allocation}

Once candidates can be constructed and evaluated, the optimization policy must select where to spend the next evaluation. When tuning an on-chip crossbar or memory interconnect, one option is to refine an arbitration scheme that has already performed well under benchmark traffic. Another is to explore a different buffering topology whose latency behavior is less certain. The first is exploitation: using what the study has learned to pursue improvement. The second is exploration: gathering information that may reveal a better alternative. A limited tool budget makes the balance consequential, because time spent on one candidate is unavailable for another.

A surrogate-guided search makes this balance explicit through an *acquisition function*, a rule that scores possible evaluations using predictions and their uncertainty. The predictor estimates what a candidate may achieve; the acquisition function expresses why evaluating it would be useful. Bayesian optimization repeats this process: fit or update a surrogate, select an evaluation using the acquisition rule, obtain a tool result, and use that observation to guide the next choice.

For a quantity being maximized, an upper-confidence-bound acquisition rule scores a candidate using $\mu(x)+\kappa\sigma(x)$, where $\mu(x)$ is the surrogate's predicted mean, $\sigma(x)$ its predictive standard deviation, and $\kappa$ the weight assigned to uncertainty. Whereas a high mean favors exploitation, a large uncertainty term can make a less-tested candidate worth examining, and for minimizing a cost such as energy the corresponding optimistic direction points toward lower values. In either case, the acquisition score sets a search priority rather than reporting a measured benefit or a guarantee of feasibility.

For a Gaussian-process surrogate, the observations determine both the predicted mean and the model's uncertainty under its chosen kernel and noise assumptions. The acquisition function turns those quantities into an evaluation priority. This separates the predictor's estimate from the optimizer's choice.

The selected point need not have the highest predicted mean. Wide predictive uncertainty can justify spending an evaluation there. Other acquisition rules target expected improvement or information gain. The choice depends on what the study needs to learn, the cost of the next observation, and whether the model's uncertainty is useful under the current search conditions (@sec-support-limits).

The rule must also respect the candidate space: when a parameter is discrete, such as set associativity in $\{2,4,8,16\}$, treating it as an unrestricted continuous variable can produce an unevaluable proposal or misleading notions of similarity, whereas Gaussian processes with suitable input transformations or kernels, tree-based models, and mixed-integer formulations preserve discrete structure. Known constraints should be enforced during construction or checked before expensive evaluation, while a topology or instruction set architecture (ISA) change that cannot be expressed in the current representation requires revising that representation before the search can consider it.

Parallel tools change how evaluations are allocated. A synchronous search can choose a batch and wait for its results; an asynchronous search can request another candidate when a slot becomes free. In either case, selection should account for evaluations already in flight, so that several slots do not unknowingly repeat the same work. Deliberate repetition can still be useful for estimating noise or confirming a close comparison. The trade-off is between using available capacity and waiting for information that might improve the next choice.

Tool feedback must retain its semantics when it enters the optimization loop, because misencoding failed or incomplete runs can teach the optimizer to exploit the failure mode (@sec-data-representations-world-models). A job terminated at a wall-clock limit yields a right-censored lower bound on completion time [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival] rather than a valid measurement of energy, area, or any other unfinished objective; while a search policy may model timeout probability separately or assign an explicit penalty to guide selection, it must keep that policy weight distinct from measured hardware outcomes and separate from infrastructure crashes or nonconvergent runs.

Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization adds a choice of evaluation fidelity to the choice of candidate [@KandasamyEtAl2017MultiFidelityBO]: a cheaper approximation is useful when its result can inform the target comparison at lower cost, although it cannot replace checks of properties it does not observe. The study must therefore retain which approximation produced each observation and reserve enough budget for reference evaluations. While these choices describe how a search spends its resources, choosing an optimization algorithm requires examining how its concrete mechanism carries out those decisions.

## Optimization Algorithms and Heuristics

Once the study has fixed an evaluation budget and sampling policy, the optimization algorithm it selects has to match the structure of the candidate space, because algorithms differ in how they construct a search, use feedback, and retain information across evaluations, and method comparisons depend on the problem, representation, and experimental conditions [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL; @KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. In spatial accelerator design, searching over discrete array dimensions differs from optimizing continuous buffer partition boundaries or navigating non-convex macro floorplan coordinates, so understanding those structural differences helps identify which mechanisms are worth comparing.

Enumeration and random search set the transparent baselines: enumeration settles a small finite space outright, and random search samples legal candidates without using earlier scores. Domain heuristics encode engineering rules, such as prioritizing transformations along a critical timing path. Local search, simulated annealing, and evolutionary search revise candidates through moves, and in hardware those moves must preserve legality or invoke a repair pass, because a mutated netlist or a crossover of two floorplans is rarely legal as produced. Bayesian optimization spends surrogate uncertainty where evaluations are expensive. Differentiable optimization follows gradients over relaxed continuous parameters, and its answer must then be projected back onto discrete registers and gates, where the projection can lose the improvement.

Mathematical programming and constraint solvers use explicit objectives and constraints to search an encoded problem, exploiting known structure without first learning a search policy even though the encoding and solution process have their own costs. Equality saturation provides a related way to retain alternatives during rewriting:[^fn-egraph-c05] whereas a greedy sequence of transformations can discard a form that would have enabled a better later rewrite, an e-graph retains equivalent forms reached through supplied rewrite rules until those rules add no new information or the search reaches its budget. An extraction pass then chooses a low-cost represented netlist or schedule using a cost model and an algorithm such as integer linear programming or dynamic programming (as implemented in the `egg` library), provided the rewrite rules preserve the intended semantics and the workflow budgets for graph growth and extraction.

[^fn-egraph-c05]: **E-graphs and equality saturation**: An e-graph (equivalence graph) compactly represents exponential numbers of equivalent algebraic or program expressions. Equality saturation applies rewrite rules monotonically while retaining earlier forms, reducing dependence on a greedy rewrite order. An extraction pass then selects a low-cost form among those represented, subject to the cost model, extraction algorithm, and search budget.

Factor-screening experiments provide another way to reduce a search before committing to many evaluations by estimating which factors have the largest effects [@PlackettBurman1946Design]. Unlike candidate screening, which filters which designs proceed to evaluation, factor screening identifies which design choices deserve attention, although its interpretation relies on interactions being small enough not to obscure those main effects. In the datapath example, where pipeline depth and resource sharing may interact strongly, screening each factor in isolation could discard a useful combination.

Reinforcement learning trains a policy to select actions from represented state using interaction rewards, which can suit sequential problems where earlier actions change later options even though sequential structure alone does not rule out conventional search or planning. Macro placement provides a prominent example: because placing a macro block changes available floorplan space and alters downstream routing congestion, a policy can select placements from the partial floorplan while feedback assesses the resulting arrangement (@fig-alphachip-placement) [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Independent assessments report that mature classical baselines, such as analytical placement and simulated annealing, matched or outperformed the reinforcement-learning placements on the designs and metrics they evaluated without pretraining a policy [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment], whereas the original authors disputed the 2023 assessment [@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed] and the 2026 update evaluates newer code and pretrained checkpoints. Because these reports leave the matched comparison contested rather than establishing a universal ranking of the methods, a learned policy must demonstrate that its returns exceed those of conventional physical-design engines under equivalent compute budgets.

![**A placement policy learns to choose actions from a partial floorplan.** In this schematic of the reinforcement-learning macro placement framework [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], the policy places macros sequentially, receiving an updated partial floorplan after each step. Once the macros are placed, an approximate standard-cell placement supports a proxy cost combining wirelength, congestion, and density; its negative supplies a terminal reward. Optimizing this reward still requires downstream checks of placement legality, routing, and timing, and rigorous comparison against classical analytical baselines [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement].](images/fig-alphachip-placement){#fig-alphachip-placement width="100%" fig-alt="Loop diagram with separate lanes for a placement policy's outbound macro-location action and the partial floorplan's inbound next state. After placing all macros, an approximate standard-cell placement precedes a density, congestion, and wirelength proxy cost, whose negative becomes the terminal reward."}

A learned placement policy incurs substantial training compute before it yields reusable decisions: because invoking a full commercial EDA implementation flow for every training interaction would add prohibitive compute and license costs, the loop relies on fast standard-cell proxy placement to approximate wirelength and congestion while deferring signoff routing and timing closure. Long action sequences with only a terminal scalar reward also make credit assignment harder, since the policy learns little about which specific macro placement caused a downstream routing congestion or timing failure. A reinforcement-learning placement loop must therefore establish that its final signoff metrics justify its upfront training overhead, and while cheap proxy rewards reduce evaluation cost and reuse across related blocks can amortize training, transfer must be demonstrated on the specific blocks that will use the policy.

For a one-off architectural decision, direct search, deterministic heuristics, or Bayesian optimization may avoid a training cost that has little opportunity to be amortized. When evaluation budgets are limited, the relevant comparison is how much confirmed improvement each method reaches before that budget runs out.

Optimization trajectories can depend strongly on budget: a greedy heuristic or local gradient search may gain quickly and then stall in a local optimum, whereas Bayesian optimization or evolutionary search may need initial exploration before overtaking it. ArchGym's comparison of search algorithms across architecture simulators found that, given unlimited samples and tuned hyperparameters, the algorithms were equally able to meet the target specification [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], so the differences that matter in practice appear at finite budgets. Comparing optimization methods therefore requires fixed evaluation budgets and identical stopping rules, since an early lead does not establish algorithmic superiority when a trajectory is overtaken before the evaluation budget expires. To serve as valid architectural evidence, comparisons must account for the full computational cost, including surrogate training and failed tool runs, rather than reporting only post-hoc candidate evaluations.

The objective also shapes the search: while minimizing energy subject to area and timing limits in the datapath is a constrained single-objective problem, a study seeking several useful trade-offs can use multi-objective optimization to retain nondominated candidates for which no other evaluated design is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. That retained set approximates the Pareto frontier over the designs examined rather than the true frontier of the entire design space, whereas a weighted scalar score encodes fixed preferences that may hide trade-off alternatives an architect would want to compare.

The mechanisms have different prerequisites and failure modes (@tbl-optimization-methods). The table summarizes where each can be useful. These are starting points for a comparison, not categorical rules that make an algorithm valid or invalid solely from its name.

| **Search procedure** | **Strong fit** | **Required conditions** | **Common mismatch** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enumeration | Small, finite legal spaces where every candidate is evaluable. | Explicit action space, affordable exhaustive coverage. | Applying after space exceeds available budget. |
| Random search / sampling | Large spaces permitting independent samples; transparent baseline. | Legal sampler, matched budget, retained failures. | Treating as insurance against flawed objectives. |
| Deterministic heuristics | Spaces with exploitable domain structure. | Explicit rules, assumptions, clear stopping rules. | Hiding manual tuning or biasing search away from optimal regions. |
| Simulated annealing | Spaces with useful local moves and multiple local optima. | Legal neighborhood, acceptance and temperature schedules, evaluation budget. | Moves or cooling schedules that leave little opportunity to reach better regions. |
| Bayesian optimization | Costly evaluations where a surrogate can guide selection from limited observations. | Suitable representation, useful uncertainty estimates, acquisition rule, evaluation budget. | A surrogate or acquisition rule poorly matched to the candidate space or changing feedback. |
| Differentiable optimization | Continuous parameters or trustworthy relaxations. | Useful gradients, post-discretization verification. | Ignoring discretization gaps, yielding unrealizable hardware. |
| Evolutionary search | Discrete/mixed spaces with population variation operators. | Legal mutation/crossover or repair, sufficient evaluations for the population. | Too few evaluations to improve the population or weak comparison baselines. |
| Reinforcement learning | Sequential choices where learning a policy can repay its interaction cost. | Informative state, meaningful rewards, affordable training, demonstrated reuse when needed. | Paying to train a policy for a problem that direct search resolves more cheaply. |
| Mathematical programming / solvers | Algebraic objectives, discrete choices, explicit constraints. | Formalizable objectives and constraints. | Optimizing unrepresented architectural desiderata. |
: **Search mechanisms differ in the structure and feedback they require.** Suitability depends on the candidate representation, available evaluations, and cost of fitting or tuning the procedure. {#tbl-optimization-methods tbl-colwidths="[22,26,26,26]"}

Learned optimizers must be benchmarked against simple baselines (enumeration, random search, or domain heuristics) under identical spaces and tool budgets [@BergstraBengio2012RandomSearch]. PrefixRL illustrates this discipline in arithmetic circuit synthesis by integrating logic synthesis directly into its evaluation loop [@RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL].

Because commercial and open-source synthesis transformations, HLS autotuners, and placement engines already combine extensive domain heuristics with mathematical solvers, beating random search alone does not demonstrate an advantage over practical engineering baselines. Establishing a net gain requires comparing the proposed optimizer against a well-tuned conventional tool flow under matched conditions (or documenting why that comparator was unavailable) and counting setup and tuning overhead alongside the final improvement.

Stopping criteria likewise belong in the study formulation before the search begins: a loop may halt when a candidate meets declared improvement and feasibility targets, when the evaluation or tool-time budget is exhausted (charging failed and incomplete runs against the budget they consume), or when the expected value of further search no longer justifies another batch. Crossing an acceptance threshold establishes a sufficient design for the study rather than a global optimum, whereas exhausting the budget without a feasible candidate leaves open whether a larger budget or a different formulation would succeed.

For a compact comparison of supplied cache capacities, a fixed run limit can bound the work, with earlier stopping only if the declared comparison and feasibility checks resolve the capacity decision. For the datapath, acceptance might require confirmed energy improvement while meeting throughput, area, and timing constraints. Each rule connects the search to a decision rather than to an indefinite pursuit of a better score. Putting such a budget into practice also requires knowing how much evaluation the available tools can provide.

## Evaluation Capacity and Screening Cost {#sec-method-evaluation-costs}

A method must fit the evaluation resources available to the study. Two calculations help assess that fit: how quickly the tools can process candidates, and how much reference evaluation a cheaper screen can reliably avoid. These limits apply whether candidates come from a conventional search, a learned generator, or a combination.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Quantifying Evaluation Capacity {#sec-sample-efficiency-under-expensive-feedback}

Producing a candidate creates work for the tools that evaluate it. A generator may draft a hardware implementation quickly, while simulation and physical implementation take much longer. An optimizer can create the same mismatch by requesting evaluations faster than the tools finish them (@sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search). Choosing a useful proposal rate requires counting both the evaluations each tool can complete and the fraction of candidates that reach it.

Evaluation paths often begin with cheaper checks that eliminate unsuitable candidates before more expensive work. Analytical rooflines test encoded bounds; Spike checks functional execution; gem5 models cycle-level contention. Implementation questions require other checks, such as STA in OpenSTA, power analysis under UPF intent, and SVA checked with BMC.[^fn-eda-signoff-c05] These tools establish different properties. The path must be chosen for the design question; a faster check cannot replace a slower one that establishes a different property.

[^fn-eda-signoff-c05]: **Signoff tools**: OpenSTA checks modeled circuit paths against declared timing constraints. UPF specifies power intent, such as voltage domains and power gating, for tools that analyze or verify it. SVA expresses properties; BMC checks them over a specified bounded execution horizon. In production physical signoff, these checks are coupled with physical design rule check (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS) verification using foundry rule decks in qualified tools, such as Siemens Calibre or Synopsys IC Validator. A commercial 3\ nm implementation claim therefore needs an applicable foundry-qualified signoff path. The Lighthouse cache plan has not established such a path; producing a layout in an academic flow would not supply it.

The number of possible candidates can greatly exceed that path's capacity. A single GPU operator's schedule space in AutoTVM can reach billions of implementations [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], and the accelerator mapping spaces modeled with MAESTRO and Timeloop are likewise far too large for exhaustive evaluation [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO; @ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Such spaces motivate pruning and selective evaluation. Even a small candidate set, however, can be costly if each evaluation is slow; candidate count and evaluation cost must be considered together.

Improving candidate quality can also increase the downstream load: at an unchanged proposal rate, a generator whose outputs pass early checks more often sends more work to later tools. While spare downstream capacity lets those tools evaluate more promising candidates, a stage that is already near capacity will instead accumulate a growing backlog, so the operational question is how the changed pass rates affect arrivals at each stage.

To see how upstream pass rates constrain the sustainable proposal rate $g$, we can model the evaluation path as a sequence of tool stages. For this calculation, assume fixed mean runtimes and conditional pass rates, separate capacity at each stage, and no retries or returning candidates.[^fn-feedback-c05] Stage $i$ has $c_i$ parallel slots and mean runtime $t_i$, giving a service capacity $\mu_i = c_i/t_i$, while its conditional pass rate $p_i$ is the fraction of inputs that advance to stage $i+1$.

[^fn-feedback-c05]: **Returning work in queueing models**: Retries and repeated evaluations add visits to tool stages. A model with returning work must include those visits in each stage's arrival rate; the one-pass product used here does not include them.

Because only candidates that clear all preceding stages reach stage $i$, its offered arrival rate is $\lambda_i = g \prod_{j=1}^{i-1}p_j$ (with the empty product at $i=1$ equal to one, since every proposal enters the first stage). Comparing incoming work with available service capacity via the utilization ratio $\rho_i = \lambda_i/\mu_i < 1$ at every stage yields the stability bound in @eq-queue-stability-bound [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]:

$$
g < \min_i \left( \frac{\mu_i}{\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j} \right).
$${#eq-queue-stability-bound}

The minimum identifies the bottleneck stage that saturates first as proposals increase. Because the denominator $\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j$ is the cumulative survival probability through stage $i-1$, improving a generator so that more of its proposals pass early lint or compile checks *increases* that denominator and therefore *reduces* the maximum proposal rate $g$ that downstream simulation or synthesis stages can sustain. This is a steady-flow bound rather than a prediction of turnaround time: bursty arrivals and variable runtimes can cause queuing delays well below the bound, a finite study may finish before a steady regime develops, and shared license pools or retries require additional accounting.

The conditional pass rates also determine how much of the proposed work clears the entire path. Expected finalist throughput across an $M$-stage pipeline, while every stage remains below capacity, is:

$$
q = g \prod_{i=1}^M p_i.
$${#eq-finalist-throughput}

The final pass rate $p_M$ affects the output rate in @eq-finalist-throughput, but not the work entering the final stage: candidates consume that stage's service before they pass or fail. A finalist has cleared the modeled checks; choosing a design still requires comparison with the baseline and any further checks needed for the intended use.

Higher pass rates can improve finalist yield while increasing downstream load. For example, a generator whose RTL passes the structural screen more often sends more work to simulation at the same proposal rate. If simulation or implementation already limits the path, the sustainable proposal rate falls unless its service capacity also increases. Better proposals can therefore require tighter admission control even as they improve the quality of the designs reaching expensive tools.

Applying @eq-queue-stability-bound requires observed service times, conditional pass rates, and available parallel capacity from the intended tool flow. The execution record should distinguish time spent running from time waiting, and count failed evaluations and repeat visits. If sustained arrivals exceed a stage's service capacity, an unlimited queue grows; a bounded system must delay, block, or reject submissions. The equation identifies the load to control, while measurements establish where that limit lies for the actual study.

The execution harness can regulate submissions by limiting batch sizes or the number of outstanding evaluations. Token-bucket or leaky-bucket admission control provides other ways to enforce a rate limit. These controls act on candidate requests; a language model's token generation rate alone does not specify its demand for tool evaluations. Increasing filtering can reduce demand too, but only if the revised screen retains the candidates needed for the study's decision.

For method selection, this calculation identifies where additional capability could help. Faster proposals are useful when the evaluation path can absorb them. When it cannot, the study may need fewer proposals, more evaluation capacity, or a reliable cheaper screen. The last option raises a separate question: how much expensive work can screening actually save?

### Screening Cost and Validated Coverage

A cheap screen can reduce the work sent to an expensive evaluator, but running quickly is useful only when it also resolves enough cases reliably. In on-chip SRAM or accelerator pipeline design, an early analytical area screen might immediately reject an implementation that exceeds maximum floorplan boundaries while routing any candidate near the boundary to a reference placement evaluation. The net saving therefore depends on how often the screen can settle a comparison within the study's allowed error and on what it costs to verify that the screening rule remains reliable.

Selective classification studies the trade-off between the fraction of cases a model answers and its error on those answers; it permits the model to abstain on the remaining cases [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. For architectural screening, *validated coverage* $f$ is the fraction of the target comparison stream that a qualified screening rule settles without the reference evaluation, under declared error limits. It is not simply the fraction of candidates rejected. A rule that rejects many useful designs may save tool time while defeating the purpose of the search.

To calculate the possible saving, count *service work*: the evaluation effort spent processing comparisons, excluding time waiting in queues. Let $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$ be the reference cost per comparison and $c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ the cost of a cheap check, measured in the same units. This simplified model assigns a common reference cost to cases that are screened out and cases that proceed. If their costs differ systematically, the calculation must instead weight the work saved in each group.

Suppose a fraction $a$ of all comparisons receives a cheap check and a fraction $f \le a$ is settled there: because the fraction $a-f$ pays for both checks while the fraction $1-a$ goes directly to the reference path, a total share $1-f$ still incurs the reference cost. Screening adds $a c_{\mathrm{cheap}}$ per original comparison together with routing, qualification, auditing, and rework overhead, which we denote by $\epsilon \ge 0$ after normalizing by $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$. Dividing the original reference cost by the resulting total cost gives:

$$
S_{\mathrm{screen}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + a \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon} \le \frac{1}{(1-f) + f \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon}.
$${#eq-screening-efficiency-bound}

For fixed coverage and costs, @eq-screening-efficiency-bound is largest when every cheap check settles its case ($a=f$). This is an ideal routing bound; in practice, screening outcomes cannot be determined before the check executes. Universal screening uses $a=1$ and pays the cheap-check cost on every comparison, including those that subsequently need the reference path.

Even if screening and its overhead become free, the remaining fraction $1-f$ still pays full reference cost. The speedup therefore approaches $1/(1-f)$, following the same unaffected-work argument as Amdahl's law [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. For fixed coverage below one, reducing screening cost cannot exceed this ceiling. The screen can also make the process more expensive if its cost and overhead exceed the reference work it avoids.

A structural legality screen illustrates why rejection rate and validated coverage differ. Rejected RTL can bypass simulation when the structural defect is sufficient to disqualify it under the study's rules. A predictor that rejects a design merely because its estimated performance is poor needs evidence that this choice does not discard useful candidates. The fraction rejected establishes neither the reliability of that decision nor the resulting saving.

To use the bound in a study, estimate coverage and screening error on a representative sample of the whole target stream. Checking only the cases the screen chose to settle leaves performance on the omitted cases unknown and can introduce selection bias [@Heckman1979SampleSelectionBias]. Report the sampling procedure, uncertainty in the coverage estimate, and errors that matter to the decision, especially rejection of useful candidates. Shared assumptions between the screen and reference can hide errors from both; agreement establishes only what that reference path can check.

Whereas the capacity model bounds how much candidate traffic each tool stage can serve, the screening model estimates how much reference evaluation work a cheap filter can avoid. Even when a screen reduces total service work, translating that reduction into shorter wall-clock turnaround still depends on queuing behavior, parallel slot availability, and unmodeled setup costs, and validated coverage must be rechecked whenever the candidate distribution or hardware–software stack shifts (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). Together, the two bounds establish whether composing methods can save work or improve results within the available budget.

## Composing Prediction, Generation, and Optimization {#sec-one-model-specialists-hybrid}

A search procedure needs candidates or actions to select, and feedback with which to compare them. Generation can construct those candidates; prediction can estimate properties that are expensive to evaluate. Composing these methods is useful when their contributions improve the study together. It does not require every study to use all three families.

In an illustrative redesign of the Lighthouse arithmetic datapath (sketched here as a prospective loop rather than a completed experiment), a generator proposes a new arithmetic organization or pipeline staging under the required computation and interface constraints. Once a candidate clears initial structural and functional checks, a qualified surrogate estimates its post-synthesis area and delay so that an optimizer can weigh those predictions against prior observations and the remaining budget before dispatching an expensive implementation run, whose returned energy, area, and timing measurements then guide the next selection or revision request.

How the loop responds depends on which component the feedback implicates: a timing violation points back to a revised pipeline structure, whereas a large surrogate residual requires evaluating similar candidates directly or recalibrating the predictor before trusting its rankings again. Because newly generated topologies can fall outside the predictor's support even when they are functionally correct, all three components must share candidate identities and evaluation conditions while keeping surrogate estimates strictly distinct from tool-checked results.

The roles need not correspond to separate models or occur once in a fixed order: while an evolutionary procedure can both construct variants and select among them, a neural generator can work alongside symbolic solvers or static compiler passes that enforce encoded constraints. AutoTVM and Ansor provide concrete examples of composing search with learned cost models for tensor programs [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor], although their compositions serve those specific tensor-scheduling formulations rather than establishing a universal sequence for architecture design.

As a loop grows, it may also need repair, diagnosis, and coordination. The distinctions in @tbl-method-role-handoffs specify what each job produces and how another component can use it. They describe responsibilities that a human, a conventional tool, or a learned component might perform.

| **Engineering role** | **Concrete output** | **Next check or handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proposal** | Named candidate or experiment request with identified changes. | Verify legality and scope before invoking expensive tools. |
| **Screening** | Scoped estimate or ranking with predicted properties and uncertainty. | Route selected candidates to measurement path; retain predictions for qualification. |
| **Search** | Next candidate or experiment, selection basis, remaining budget. | Execute within the current search formulation; make any proposed change to that formulation explicit. |
| **Static Analysis** | Testable defect, missing assumption, or conflict tied to named artifact. | Use the finding to guide revision; check whether the revised candidate resolves it. |
| **Repair** | Revised artifact linked to parent and modification record. | Treat as fresh candidate; rerun affected checks. |
| **Checking** | Result from named check under declared conditions (including timeouts/failures). | Interpret what the check establishes and what remains untested (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). |
| **Diagnostic Localization** | Proposed mechanism and distinguishing contrast conditions. | Request targeted measurement; analysis does not substitute for verification. |
| **Coordination** | Ordered request graph with dependencies, budgets, and artifact IDs. | Hand requests to environment for tool orchestration. |
: **Each engineering role produces an output that another role can use.** Separating proposals, estimates, revisions, and checked results makes their different contributions explicit. {#tbl-method-role-handoffs tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

The repair row illustrates why these distinctions matter. A revised datapath is a new candidate: the earlier timing result belongs to its parent and cannot be carried forward as if no design change occurred. Likewise, a diagnosis suggests what to investigate, while a targeted check tests that explanation. A component can perform several roles, but its outputs still need to preserve these differences.

To simplify the datapath loop, we start by asking which work is actually needed: when a few candidate implementations already exist and direct evaluation is affordable, neither generation nor a learned screen is necessary, whereas when candidate construction is required but each design is cheap to evaluate, generation and optimization can rely on direct tool feedback. Only when individual evaluations take days can a learned predictor make a comparable result cheaper or help find a better design within the same budget, provided its net benefit accounts for data collection, fitting, inference, qualification, and reference confirmation.

These alternatives lead to different compositions (@tbl-method-organization), and the table notes where each typically sits among the operational layers of @sec-three-operational-layers. A conventional baseline may already predict, construct candidates, or search. Conventional versus learned describes the technique, whereas prediction, generation, and optimization describe what the method does. Here, "generation only" means generation is the only added method family beyond that baseline. Compilation, checking, and evaluation are still required, and the same convention applies to the other rows.

| **Composition** | **Typical operational layer** | **When justified** | **What must be established** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct tools / conventional technique | Conventional baseline | Analytical models, solvers, or direct simulations perform work economically. | Retain unless an added component improves result quality or total cost while preserving checks. |
| Generation only | Typically Layer 1 point assistance | New or revised artifacts are needed; direct checking is affordable. | Generated candidates meet the intended requirements at an acceptable construction and checking cost. |
| Prediction only | Any layer; screening within a study | Candidates require cheap screening before expensive simulation. | Achieve comparable results at lower total cost or better supported results at the same budget, including fitting, inference, qualification, and confirmation costs. |
| Optimization only | Typically Layer 2 parameter search | Selecting among existing candidates or legal actions requires a search. | Benchmark against simple baselines; stop when further search yields diminishing returns. |
| Generation + prediction | Layer 1 drafting with a screen | Candidate construction and cheap screening are useful before expensive evaluation. | Predictor has support for the generated structures; selected candidates receive the required confirmation. |
| Generation + optimization | Layer 2, or Layer 3 for coordinated revisions beyond the template | Candidate construction required under selective search budget without supported surrogate. | Optimizer uses direct tool feedback; generated candidates pass verification. |
| Prediction + optimization | Typically Layer 2 surrogate search | Surrogate enables selective search under expensive tool feedback. | Keep surrogate, acquisition rule, and confirmation stages separately inspectable. |
| Generation + prediction + optimization | Candidate for Layer 3; not required by it | Constructing alternatives, estimating consequences, and directing search each improve the study. | Their combined benefit exceeds fitting, integration, and checking costs at the required result quality. |
: **Pipeline components must earn their cost in the declared study.** Each composition addresses particular work and introduces qualification, integration, and checking costs. The layer column indicates typical placement, not a requirement; no composition confers a layer by itself. {#tbl-method-organization tbl-colwidths="[20,20,30,30]"}

Although an AI-native design system will often compose all three families, composing them does not by itself make a workflow AI-native unless it also supports revising candidate structures across abstraction boundaries with checks matched to the claimed result, including implementation and signoff evidence whenever physical readiness is claimed. The public report examined in @sec-design-conductor-case carries generated designs through a physical implementation flow, yet it neither establishes foundry signoff nor compares total cost against a matched conventional flow, leaving open whether such a system reaches a comparable, physically realizable result at lower total cost.

The generation-plus-optimization row fits a datapath search that constructs alternatives and evaluates them directly. Adding prediction is a separate decision, justified only if the screen improves that search at the available budget. The rows therefore describe alternatives rather than an automatic mandate to deploy every method. The compiler and cache studies apply this reasoning to two different candidate spaces and evaluation costs.

## Method Selection in Two Contrasting Studies

Two studies can both aim to select a better implementation and still need different methods. Tensor-program tuning may involve more schedules than can be measured on the target hardware, while the prospective mobile system-on-chip (SoC) cache study compares only three capacities. Their contrast makes method selection concrete: how many alternatives need evaluation, where will useful observations come from, and what can the budget cover?

### Compiler Tuning versus Cache Evaluation

For a fixed tensor operator and hardware target, a schedule determines implementation choices such as loop order, tiling, and parallel execution. AutoTVM combines a learned cost model with search over these choices. Selected programs run on the target hardware, and their measured runtimes supply observations for updating the model [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Compatible observations from earlier workloads can help, but a preexisting training dataset is not required; observations can accumulate during tuning.

The reason to learn a cost model is that relatively few measured schedules may help prioritize many unmeasured ones. That benefit must repay the measurements used to learn the model as well as fitting and inference. A large schedule space creates an opportunity for selective search, but does not by itself show that a learned model improves on conventional tuning.

The illustrative cache study instead proposes three discrete capacity settings (2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB) under a budget intended to cover direct static random-access memory (SRAM) screening and cycle-level simulation. Because no matching prior data exists, collecting measurements to train a surrogate would consume the same small evaluation budget, making direct evaluation the proposed starting method (@tbl-worked-method-decisions). While that plan still uses analytical models and simulation to estimate hardware behavior without adding a learned surrogate, execution remains pending.

| **Decision parameter** | **Tensor-program tuning plan** | **Illustrative cache study** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Job** | Select a schedule that improves operator runtime on the target hardware. | Compare 2\ MiB baseline against 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB without expanding scope. |
| **Inputs and support** | Fixed operator and target, legal schedules, compiler version, evaluation budget, measurements collected during tuning; compatible prior data if available. | Three proposed `l2.capacity` settings, hardware/software specifications, SRAM constraints, no prior matching data. |
| **Approach status** | Search and learned cost modeling, following the AutoTVM pattern; study-specific comparator and budget still required. | Analytical SRAM screening followed by matched cycle-level simulations of the supplied candidates; no added generator or learned surrogate. |
| **Output and legal actions** | Selected legal schedule with checked correctness and measured target runtime. | Modeled SRAM metrics and matched cycle-level simulation results for 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, or 4\ MiB only. |
| **Evaluator and checks** | Compile and check outputs against the operator specification; measure runtime under matched target conditions. | SRAM physical model checks limits; cycle-level simulation and power models return system metrics. |
| **Feedback cost** | Surrogate fitting, candidate compilation, target runs, tuning review. | Three SRAM evaluations, maximum four cycle-level runs. |
| **Fallback and stop** | Compare with an applicable default schedule or tuned operator implementation; set the measurement budget and stopping criteria. | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulate performance while keeping physical feasibility unresolved. Stop at the declared decision or budget limit. |
: **Candidate space, available data, and feedback cost distinguish the method choices.** A large compiler schedule space can justify surrogate-guided search, whereas the proposed three-capacity cache comparison favors direct evaluation. The compiler plan draws on a published method; this comparison reports no new execution results. {#tbl-worked-method-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The inputs and feedback-cost rows explain the contrast: whereas observations collected from a subset of schedules in the compiler study can guide selection across many others, obtaining training observations in the three-capacity cache study would already perform much of the direct comparison. Method selection therefore follows how much useful search work remains after data collection. Although that conclusion would change if the cache question expanded to many interacting design parameters or if a qualified surrogate already existed, the current question requires only an explicit evaluation plan specifying how the three capacities will be compared and what the results can establish.

### Evaluation Protocol and Resource Budgeting

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Lighthouse Cache Evaluation Plan"}
**Context.** The question is whether increasing cache capacity from 2\ MiB to 3\ MiB or 4\ MiB reduces frame time while meeting the subsystem's power limit and the cache's area and access-time limits.

**Application.** Evaluate the supplied capacities directly. First assess each cache organization with an analytical SRAM model, then compare candidates through matched cycle-level simulations. No learned surrogate is proposed for this small comparison.

**Outcome.** This is an evaluation plan, not an executed result. The physical models and simulator configuration still need to be established before the plan can determine feasibility or a preferred capacity.
:::

The plan must connect a capacity setting to the hardware it represents. A larger cache may reduce misses, but it also changes storage area, leakage, and potentially access latency. Holding the workload and unrelated design choices fixed makes the comparison interpretable; holding these capacity-dependent consequences fixed would hide part of the trade-off. Each setting therefore needs a corresponding organization and a consistent rule for deriving its modeled properties.

The proposed limits in @tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision make that comparison specific. TSMC N3E is the chosen implementation target, not an available, validated technology model. Before relying on an SRAM estimate, the study must establish that its model and parameters support the target process and candidate organizations.

| **Plan detail** | **Lighthouse cache comparison** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Selected approach** | Direct evaluation with no added learned components. |
| **Allowed change** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold workload, software, and unrelated microarchitectural choices fixed; derive capacity-dependent organization and timing consistently. |
| **Required tool roles** | A suitable SRAM model estimates cache macro area, access time, and leakage for the target conditions. A configured gem5 simulation provides frame-time and miss-rate estimates; compatible power models estimate subsystem power. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level runs, including failed or repeated attempts. This is a proposed limit, not a demonstrated sufficient budget. |
| **Feasibility checks** | Check functional behavior and candidate identity. Require modeled subsystem power at or below $3\ \text{W}$, total cache macro area at or below $1.5\ \text{mm}^2$, and access time at or below $2.5\ \text{ns}$. Physical feasibility additionally requires implementation timing, power analysis (including declared power intent), and physical signoff checks (DRC and LVS) across characterized process corners. |
| **Performance comparison** | Compare frame time against the 2\ MiB baseline under matched conditions. Define how uncertainty will be assessed before execution; accept an improvement only when the resulting interval for baseline minus candidate frame time is positive. |
| **Fallback and stopping** | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulation can still compare performance under explicit cache assumptions, but physical feasibility remains unresolved. Stop when the declared comparison is resolved or the budget is exhausted; report an inconclusive result if the available evidence does not separate the candidates. |
: **Direct evaluation gives the proposed cache comparison a concrete starting plan.** The small candidate set motivates the method choice, while the listed models, checks, and budget identify what must be established before a result can support that choice. {#tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The budget row is tight, because comparing three capacities within four runs leaves little room for failures, repeated baselines, or additional workload observations, and a run count alone does not establish the uncertainty of a frame-time difference. When the planned observations cannot separate a candidate's improvement from comparison uncertainty, the study must either report an inconclusive outcome or secure a revised budget rather than treating the lowest observed frame time as a reliable winner simply because the budget is exhausted.

This is a fixed design path in the sense of @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales. Results select among supplied capacities rather than generate a revised organization. That scope is sufficient for the question being asked. @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces examines the physical definitions and tool setup needed to execute such plans, while @sec-what-architect-owns explains why halting before dispatch preserves engineering integrity when prerequisites remain incomplete.

Total cost also extends beyond the evaluations themselves (@tbl-method-role-limits), since configuring gem5, establishing the cache and power models, obtaining applicable licenses, and reviewing results all consume engineering resources before any learned component is added. Because introducing a surrogate would require data collection and qualification on top of that baseline setup, the plan identifies no expected saving that warrants those additions for a three-candidate comparison, while across broader studies estimating when such additions will repay their cost remains an open methods question.

## Open Questions

The chapter explains what the method families contribute, but leaves open how reliably their benefits can be anticipated as a design search develops.

- **When does learning improve on an analytical model or conventional search?** Analytical models can expose the dominant constraints without collecting training data, while learned models can capture relationships missing from those approximations. The difficulty is knowing whether those missing relationships could change the design choice before spending the budget needed to learn them. A hybrid that learns a correction to an analytical model is another possibility. How can early observations distinguish a problem that benefits from learning from one better served by refining the analytical model or continuing direct search?

- **How can prediction remain reliable as optimization changes the candidates being evaluated?** A surrogate that performs well on held-out examples may become less useful when search concentrates on its most optimistic predictions or moves beyond the designs represented in its data (@sec-support-limits). Selection bias can arise even within familiar regions, while detecting unfamiliar inputs addresses a different part of the problem.[^fn-ood-c05] Shrinkage, calibrated intervals, and new reference evaluations can each help under suitable assumptions, but their value depends on the evolving search. How should the method choose between correcting predictions, collecting more observations, and relying on direct evaluation when the predicted gain is small relative to the uncertainty?

- **How can generation reach structurally different, useful designs?** Even when a representation permits many organizations, a generator may repeatedly produce similar structures. Grammar-constrained decoding and repair can increase the fraction of valid outputs without necessarily widening the set of useful designs reached. The unresolved issue is how these mechanisms interact with sampling to produce functionally correct, structurally varied designs that survive implementation checks within a fixed budget. Would broader generation reveal better trade-offs, or would it mostly increase the cost of checking unsuccessful candidates?

- **How should search allocate evaluations as its bottlenecks change?** The stability bound (@eq-queue-stability-bound) limits the proposal rate for given pass rates and service capacities, but it does not determine the most useful way to spend the remaining budget. Better proposals may send more candidates to expensive evaluation, while a stronger screen consumes work to establish which candidates it can assess reliably. The method must choose among generating alternatives, obtaining more accurate feedback, and improving the screen with only partial knowledge of their returns. When should those choices change during a search, and how can a policy avoid spending its budget improving a component that no longer limits the result?

- **When does combining methods improve the design outcome over a simpler workflow?** The compositions in @tbl-method-organization assign complementary jobs, but improvements to individual components need not combine into a better search. A generator may produce structures that its predictor cannot rank, or an optimizer may concentrate evaluations on a narrow subset of the generator's output. Whether separate component improvements or joint adaptation better address these interactions remains a question for the complete design loop. Under what workload and budget conditions does the combination retain an advantage after data collection, qualification, integration, and repair costs are included?

## Summary

Building a design system begins with the work the architecture question requires: whereas the Lighthouse datapath example may need new implementations, estimates of their consequences, and a strategy for deciding which to evaluate, the three-capacity cache comparison can start with supplied candidates and direct evaluation. Because that contrast stems from the candidate space, available information, and cost of obtaining useful feedback, understanding those conditions makes method choice an engineering decision rather than a preference for a particular model.

Prediction, generation, and optimization contribute different capabilities, and each introduces assumptions that affect the others. A generated structure may lie beyond a predictor's useful range; an optimizer may favor a predictor's errors; a better proposal process may overwhelm the tools needed to evaluate its output. A useful composition must account for these interactions as well as the strengths of its individual methods.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Match the mechanism to the work.** Distinguish the engineering role, method family, and concrete technique. Choose using the candidate representation, available data, feedback cost, and required checks; conventional algorithms and analytical models remain part of the choice.
- **Prediction guides evaluation within its supported range.** A surrogate can rank candidates or screen properties before expensive evaluation. The optimizer's curse can favor optimistic errors even among familiar designs. Qualification must reflect how predictions are used, and selected improvements need confirmation against the relevant reference evaluation.
- **Generation introduces new designs into the loop.** A generator can construct or revise an organization, rather than only select parameter values for a fixed one. Its representation, construction rules, and sampling determine which alternatives it reaches; syntax, functional behavior, and implementation constraints require distinct checks.
- **Optimization uses feedback to direct the search.** Search mechanisms differ in how they use structure, previous observations, and uncertainty. Match the mechanism to the legal actions and evaluation budget, account for downstream capacity and the cost and validated coverage of screening, and define stopping conditions that permit an inconclusive result.
- **Compose methods where their interaction helps.** Prediction, generation, and optimization are complementary capabilities, not mandatory stages or necessarily separate models, and composing all three does not by itself make a workflow AI-native. Compare any combination against a credible simpler workflow at matched total cost, including data collection, fitting, qualification, failures, and repair. Keep candidates, predictions, and checked results distinguishable as feedback moves between components.
:::

A selected method still needs a way to act on real tools. Candidate representations must become executable requests, evaluations must run under the intended conditions, and results and failures must return to the search without losing their meaning. The execution environment that makes this possible is the subject of @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces.
